final_proof:
Let \(f:\mathbb R\to L\) be a diffeomorphism; this entails no loss of generality, since every open interval is diffeomorphic to \(\mathbb R\). We regard \(f\) as a map into \(X\). Under the standard meaning of a subset diffeomorphic to an interval, \(L\) is an embedded one-dimensional submanifold of the one-dimensional manifold \(X\). An embedded submanifold having the same dimension as its ambient manifold is open: indeed, in an embedded-submanifold chart, there are no transverse coordinates that can be set equal to zero. Thus \(L\) is open in \(X\), and \(f:\mathbb R\to X\) is an injective local homeomorphism.

We first prove an endpoint observation. Suppose that \(t_n\to+\infty\) and \(f(t_n)\to p\) for some \(p\in X\setminus L\). Choose a coordinate neighborhood \(W\) of \(p\) and a coordinate map \(\phi:W\to(-3,3)\) such that \(\phi(p)=0\). Put

\[
U=\phi^{-1}((-2,2)),\qquad V=\phi^{-1}((-1,1)).
\]

Notice that \(\overline U=\phi^{-1}([-2,2])\): the displayed set is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff manifold \(X\), and it contains the closure of \(U\), while the reverse inclusion is immediate. In particular, \(\partial U=\phi^{-1}(\{-2,2\})\).

Consider a connected component \(C=(a,b)\) of the open subset \(f^{-1}(U)\subseteq\mathbb R\), and suppose that \(C\) meets \(f^{-1}(V)\). We claim that \(C\) cannot have both endpoints finite. If \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), maximality of \(C\), together with continuity of \(f\), gives \(f(a),f(b)\in\partial U\). The function \(\phi\circ f:C\to(-2,2)\) is continuous and injective, so it is strictly monotone. Its limits at the two endpoints are therefore the two distinct values \(-2\) and \(2\). (They cannot be the same value for a strictly monotone function.) The intermediate value theorem would then give some \(s\in C\) for which \(\phi(f(s))=0\), and hence \(f(s)=p\), contrary to \(p\notin L\). This proves the claim.

Every component of \(f^{-1}(U)\) meeting \(f^{-1}(V)\) is consequently unbounded above or unbounded below. There is at most one component of each kind, since two disjoint intervals cannot both be unbounded in the same direction. For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(f(t_n)\in V\). As \(t_n\to+\infty\), these \(t_n\) cannot lie in a component that is bounded above, so they lie in the unique component unbounded above. That component has the form \((a,+\infty)\) (with \(a\) possibly \(-\infty\)). On it, \(\phi\circ f\) is bounded and strictly monotone, and thus has a limit as \(t\to+\infty\). Its values along \(t_n\) tend to \(0\), so this limit is \(0\). Therefore

\[
\lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)=p.
\]

It follows in particular that at most one point of \(X\setminus L\) can be the limit of a sequence \(f(t_n)\) with \(t_n\to+\infty\), because limits in the Hausdorff space \(X\) are unique. The identical argument, with \(t\to-\infty\), shows that at most one point of \(X\setminus L\) can arise from the negative end.

Now let \(p\in\overline L\setminus L\). A manifold is first countable, so there is a sequence \(y_n\in L\) with \(y_n\to p\). Write \(y_n=f(t_n)\). The sequence \((t_n)\) has no bounded subsequence: otherwise some bounded subsequence would have a further subsequence converging to a real number \(t\), and continuity would yield \(y_n\to f(t)\in L\) along that subsequence, contradicting uniqueness of the limit and \(p\notin L\). Hence, after passing to a subsequence, either \(t_n\to+\infty\) or \(t_n\to-\infty\). Thus every point of \(\overline L\setminus L\) is associated with one of the two ends of \(\mathbb R\), and, by the endpoint observation, each end is associated with at most one such point. Consequently

\[
|\overline L\setminus L|\le 2,
\]

as claimed.
